'''Moriya clan''' (守矢氏) is a Japanese clan originating from [[Suwa District, Shinano Province]] (modern [[Suwa Region|Suwa region]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]). The clan traditionally served as the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), or chief Shinto priest, of the [[:en:Suwa Grand Shrine|Suwa Grand Shrine]]'s Upper Shrine, forming a hereditary line of shrine officials.

== Origins ==

[[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|170px|thumb|center|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Moriya Family Genealogy'' (from [[Moreya|Moreya no Kami]] to Yagushi no Kami).]]
The historical founder of the clan is unclear. According to family tradition, they are descendants of [[Moreya|Moreya no Kami]], a terrestrial deity who opposed [[Takeminakata]] (Suwa Myōjin) during his conquest of the region.

The ''Shincho Moriya Genealogy'' (神長守矢氏系譜), compiled in the early Meiji period, states that Moreya no Kami had two children: [[Morotaku no Kami]] and [[Tamamoru Hime]]. Tamamoru Hime married [[Izuhaya no Mikoto]]
, a child of Takeminakata, while Morotaku no Kami fathered [[Chikatsu no Kami]], who became Moreya's ritual successor.<ref name="Moriyakeifu">{{Cite book|lang=ja|title=Shincho Moriya Genealogy|editor=Suwa Education Society|year=1938|pages=31-72}}</ref><ref name="nomotochikato">Nomoto Sankichi, "Approach to Chikatsu no Kami," in ''Origins and Development of Suwa Faith,'' Kobuzoku Research Society, 2018, pp. 333-336.</ref>

Other records suggest that Chikatsu no Kami later moved to Uratakayama (modern [[Kanda]]) and married [[Urakohime no Mikoto]]. This lineage continued through their grandson, [[Kodamahiko-no-Mikoto]]. Thus, some interpretations argue that the Moriya clan were ritual successors to Moreya rather than direct blood descendants.

== Religious and Political Role ==

[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|180px|center|Jinchoukan Ura Kofun (Chino City), believed to be the grave of Mononobe no Moriya's son, Takemaro.]]
The Moriya clan held the hereditary title of ''jinchōkan'' or chief priest of Suwa's Upper Shrine. They were responsible for conducting sacred rituals, particularly those involving the worship of the regional spirit [[Mishaguji]].

== Cultural and Historical Legacy ==

=== Fune Kofun ===

The [[Fune Kofun]] near Moriya's stronghold is the oldest kofun (Kofun) in Suwa, dating back to the 5th century. Artifacts found include iron swords and deer antler tools, suggesting ritual significance tied to Suwa's dragon and hunting worship.<ref>{{Cite book|lang=ja|editor=Chino City|title=Chino City History: Volume I|year=1986|pages=738-740}}</ref>

=== Suwa Faith ===

The Moriya clan's traditions intertwine with the establishment of Suwa's dual governance system, where the indigenous clan (Moriya) held ritual power while the newly arrived Kami clan established administrative control. This dual structure mirrored political-religious dynamics observed in early Japanese history.

== Notable Members ==
